It can also be used to promote security in urban and rural areas and diminish fear of crime. Compared to traffic volumes during the day, there are far fewer vehicles on the roadways at night. Areas where traffic volumes and the rate of conflict between drivers and vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists remain high are typically lighted with artificial lighting systems. In 2015, there were 32,166 fatal crashes, with 28% occurring on unlit sections of roadway, a significant portion of fatalities given the low exposure compared to lighted sections (NHTSA, 2017). It is important to note that while these values are essentially the same, lighted roadways typically have a higher traffic volume and potential crash rate. Also, areas where pedestrian and cyclists are prevalent are lighted to specifications regarding their visibility and safety (IES, 2014). The number of fatal crashes on unlit roadways indicates a potential need for more lighting in rural areas or where conflict is high. Most of the lighting in rural areas is placed at intersections; however, research into other problematic areas such as certain geometries or curves could point toward more locations where increased visibility at night can save lives. The benefit of roadway lighting in general is measurable by noting the reduction in nighttime fatal crashes in areas where lighting has been implemented. The advancement of lighting technology, specifically that of SSL has opened new pathways for lighting applications on the roadway. Conventionally, roadways have incorporated high-intensity discharge (HID) lamps that operate by burning a noble gas and produce light that is of a specific color depending on the gas and salts that fill the translucent tubes within the fixture. Light-emitting diode (LED) lamps are the most common SSL technology in use on roadways. These lamps consist of diodes with electrical leads. When voltage is applied to the leads, electrons activate and recombine with electron-holes, which releases energy in the form of photons. The native light produced by this process is often whiter or bluer than those produced by common HID sources such as high-pressure sodium (HPS) or low-pressure sodium (LPS) that 2 range from light to dark yellow, amber, or even orange. LEDs create a white, broad-spectrum light that is characterized as consisting of mostly blue, as the emitted photons create short wavelengths between 450 and 480 nm. The lower operating temperature of LEDs allows them to have a longer life than vapor light sources. Additionally, the costs associated with varying the color or intensity of an LED are much lower than that of other lamp types. One of the most attractive attributes of LEDs is their propensity to reduce costs typically associated the with maintenance and replacement of HIDs.
